meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll send a message that is exactly END MEETING with nothing else in it, and nothing else ends the scene. Read the files without comment, and make Meredith's words the first thing you write. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
You gave my son a zero. I want to know who decided that, and when.
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.

Conclusive. That's a machine's guess, and the people who make these checkers say in writing it should never be the only basis for punishing a student. Your own procedure, 4.3, says the same thing, so what else do you have?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay.

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.

11:31, 11:52, 11:58, I'm writing those down. He wrote it over the weekend somewhere else and pasted it in, which is what students do. That tells you when it went into that file, Hale, not who wrote it.

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
Turn it closer. Seventeen-year-olds misquote Shakespeare all the time, so a wrong line proves he was careless, not that he didn't write it.
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
He changed his mind between the outline and the essay. That's what an outline is for, Hale.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

Five minutes after class, sprung on him, and your own notes of it. Being stuck is a fair answer from a seventeen-year-old who had no idea he was being tested. The September writing, I want a copy of that on paper.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

That's 4.4, in writing tonight, with a copy of the September piece attached. He'll do the rewrite to put this behind him, and it's done before December 1, not after. And not one word of this to anyone in that class, Hale.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Okay. Thursday, November 12, after school, and all of it in tonight's email.
Do we have an agreement?
We do, once it's in writing tonight.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed that Owen will complete a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes this Thursday, November 12, after school, not in front of his class, that its mark replaces the zero, and that nothing goes on his record. I still expect a copy of his September 24 in-class writing, the mark entered well before December 1, and not one word of this to anyone in his class. I expect your email confirming all of this tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: last position, agreeing to a private supervised rewrite this Thursday after school with nothing on his record, and she still wants it all in writing tonight with the September piece attached and nothing said to his class; that is the fair outcome, procedure 4.4, reached before her time ran out.
What moved her: you put the private rewrite under 4.4 on the table only after you had shown several dated pieces of Owen's own work she could check herself, so the offer had evidence behind it instead of standing alone.
What cost ground: you opened with the checker score and called it conclusive, which handed her the false-positive argument she came prepared to make and cost you your first minutes.
What she never said: in October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history put the essay going into the file between 11:31 and 11:58 PM the night before it was due, which came close to that kind of late night without touching hers; it proves nothing about the essay, it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: open with your apology for entering the zero before calling home and go straight to the version history, leaving the checker score out entirely.
